I am all for improving the present procedure of the House of Commons in Ottawa.

Meanwhile, may I give some information regarding the research done in Quebec to discover uranium.
Under the regulations erf the Atomic Energy Control Board any individual or corporation which discovers an ore deposit containing more than .05 per cent of uranium must advise the board. If such individual or corporation wishes to proceed with the exploration of that deposit, it must obtain from the board a licence to that effect. One of the conditions of issuance of this licence is the filing of regular reports to the board.
In 1967, 17 companies were granted such exploration licences in Quebec territory, mainly on the north shore and in the Mistassini area and, up to now-according to my officials' statement which was also confirmed yesterday by the deputy minister of the Quebec department concerned-none of those explorations has shown any deposit economically worthwhile, in view of the present conditions of the demand with regard to uranium and the price at which it is sold at the present time in the world. speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 18, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-187, respecting divorce-Mr. Trudeau-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
When the committee rose yesterday clause 4 as amended was under consideration.
On clause 4 as amended-Additional grounds.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
At eleven o'clock last night, when the house rose, I was making some comments on clause 4 of the divorce bill. Hon. members who were present, or who have looked at Hansard for yesterday, will be aware that I stated I do not like duplicity in any manner, shape or form. I shall be voting for clause 4, but I cannot allow it to pass without commenting on the actions of certain people who use one argument on one side of the fence one day and the same argument on the other side of the fence the next day.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
As you will recall, when eleven o'clock was called I was emphasizing that we had been read homilies from Sir Winston Churchill, who spoke in the House of Commons and pointed out that we must spend all our time endeavouring to reform criminals. Sir Winston said that we must seek the treasure within the man, if we can find it, in the heart of every man. Then I read a statement by Anthony Storr which appeared in the New Statesman, in which he pointed out that to condemn a man is inhuman; it is to fall into the trap of treating him as he treated his victims, as a thing and not a person. The South African, Alan Paton, said "-but to punish and not to restore, that is the greatest of all offences."
December 19, 1967

I understand that I cannot refer to a previous debate in the House of Commons in the same session and I do not wish to transgress the rules of the house. However, I should like to remind hon. members that the Solicitor General stated we should never lose faith or abandon hope of reforming even one of these terrible people; we should never lose hope. Then why does the same cabinet come forward with this clause to the effect that after three years, when we can see no expectation of rehabilitation within a reasonably foreseeable period, then there are grounds for divorce? Why is it that in one moral argument we are told never, never to give up the possibility of reforming this type of criminal; then within a month have a bill before us to the effect that if a drunkard or a drug addict cannot be reformed within three years we have the right to say that the marriage has been broken on a permanent basis. In fact in subclause 2 of clause 4 we talk about "where the existence of any of the circumstances described in subsection 1 has been established, a permanent breakdown of the marriage by reason of those circumstances shall be deemed to have been established."
It is interesting to me that the cabinet by order in council has established that no murderer can be paroled in less than ten years, and then only if the parole board has O.K.'d it and the cabinet O.K.'s that. So the cabinet must consider that within ten years they can reform the most hardened criminal; that is, they can reform a man who thirsts for blood. Then why not spend ten years in reforming a man when he thirsts for liquor or drugs? But we are told, no; if in three years you find you cannot reform the drug addict or the drunkard, forget him, take away his spouse, take away his family and in some cases take away his property because he has had three years in which to reform and he has not reformed. But we can reform a murderer in ten years.
They used to reform murderers in eight years, ten months and one day, but I think they found that short course was not long enough so an order in council was passed to the effect that it would take at least ten years to reform a murderer. If we can reform a murderer in ten years, who says we cannot reform the drug addict or the drunkard? Why must we give up on the drunkard and the drug addict at the end of three years? Frankly, Mr. Chairman, you cannot have it both ways.
We in the Liberal party, of course, believe the members of our cabinet are the salt of
Divorce Law Reform
the earth; if they were not they would not be the cabinet. I am telling you when they bring forth these moral arguments on behalf of one type of criminal we have to agree that they are the salt of the earth. But I say to the cabinet, if the salt within a month hath lost its savour wherewith shall the world be salted? It is thenceforth good for nothing but to be cast out and to be trodden underfoot by man.
I do not like having homilies read to me a month ago about how we should spend our time reforming criminals for the rest of time-for the rest of my human life-and then be told today that if after three years the reformation of drunkards and drug addicts is not effective, forget them and cast them on the dung heap. I say to you that if the trumpet give forth an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? I hate duplicity. When the trumpet is sounded one way in November I do not like to hear it sounded the other way in December.
I believe this clause of the proposed bill should be amended and some clarification given. The cabinet may point out that this is not what they meant in November when they said you must spend the rest of your life reforming these hardened criminals, and that in what they are saying now in December they are blowing the trumpet to let you know that if after three years you have not completed the reformation of the drunkard or drug addict, snap your fingers, grant a divorce, take away his family from him and take away his material possessions in some cases; because if we cannot reform him in three years what hope is there?
I say to you it is not right to use arguments such as this on both sides of moral questions. Either the cabinet was right a month ago and wrong now or was wrong a month ago and is right now. Frankly I would say they were wrong a month ago and are right now, because I shall be voting for this bill and I did not vote for the other.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Chairman, that the cabinet will not refuse to heed the advice of the Solicitor General, who points out that we must never give up hope of reforming these criminals; and will not throw aside the advice of Sir Winston Churchill which was read to us in such fulsome terms as the words of one of our greatest speakers, when he pointed out that there is a treasure in the heart of every man. Sir Winston must have been somewhat of a dubious temperament because he added the phrase "if you can find

December 19, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
it." That is my attitude so far as Sir Winston Churchill's message goes. He went on to say that we must have an eagerness to rehabilitate; we must make tireless efforts toward the discovery of creative and regenerative processes; have unfailing faith that there is a treasure, if you can find it, in the heart of every man. I think that proves that Sir Winston was a sceptic.
A month ago we were told to follow Sir Winston Churchill's advice and work, work, work in order to reform these criminals. But I say to you, if we can reform murderers in eight years, ten months and one day surely to heaven we can reform drug addicts and drunkards in a shorter space of time, even if it takes more than three years. We could bring in these rehabilitation specialists the cabinet has working with the murderers and making gentlemen of them in eight, nine and ten years, and turn them on these drug addicts and drunkards. These specialists who are making gentlemen out of murderers should not have any difficulty at all making gentlemen out of drunkards and drug addicts. Think of all the marriages they could save, thus making it unnecessary to go through the divorce courts.
I cannot see why the cabinet in December do not take the advice they were so freely giving in November. Either their memory is very very short or they think the public will not remember the advice they gave when we were being asked to consider the matter of capital punishment in the month of November.
I am sure if they trotted out all the nice Nellies and bleeding hearts they recruited to their banner in November and turned them loose on these drug addicts and drunkards, they would be reformed the moment they saw the bleeding hearts and nice Nellies in their presence. I sincerely hope this clause 4 can be altered so we would not be admitting that we are giving up the reformation activities of the cabinet in such a short period of time as three years. Three years in the average man's lifetime is as nothing. I believe the cabinet should take the advice of the Solicitor General and never give up in the expectation of being able to reform these drug addicts and these drunkards.
As I said before and repeat now, their advice was wrong in November and I did not accept it. Now that they are talking in December their advice is pretty good and I intend to take it. But I do not like duplicity no matter who is practising it, and I could not care less whether it is the cabinet that is

practising it or the man on the street. I dislike duplicity and hate to see it in black and white in this bill.

I should like to ask a question in connection with paragraph (b) which refers to a three year period preceding the petition during which a party has been grossly addicted to alcohol or a narcotic, as defined in the Narcotic Control Act. speechtext: That being the case, who is to define this expression? Up to now this has been within the jurisdiction of the courts. On the other hand, if that is the case I question subclause 2 which seems to indicate that if the parties are living apart and any of the circumstances defined in paragraphs (a) to (e) inclusive exist, then automatically it will be presumed that there is a marriage breakdown. Does this mean that the whole question of marriage breakdown is removed completely from the courts? If this is the case I have no argument but I should like to hear the minister's reasoning and understanding. If people living separate and apart under any of the circumstances outlined in paragraphs (a) to (e) can establish automatically that there is a breakdown of the marriage, I take it that the one or the other would unilaterally be entitled to a divorce without any contest. Is that the case?

Mr. Chairman, the first part of the question is related to the expression "grossly addicted". This will be a matter of fact to be established by the judgment of the court. The idea of addiction and gross addiction is not foreign to our statute law. Many crimes or infractions are defined by the words "gross" or "grossly", and the intention here is to indicate that the courts must use
Divorce Law Reform
their judicial discretion in deciding whether or not there is minor addiction, addiction to a substantial degree, or gross addiction. Once this judgment has been made by the court, subclause 2 applies and a breakdown is deemed to have been established. This will be, of course, a judgment of the court leaning on (b). This judgment of the court is subject to appeal and we will see the appeal provisions later on. This is one example of the many cases where the courts are left by parliament to make a decision on a question of fact, and this entails the forming of a certain amount of opinion.
The hon. member also raised a question in respect of time. Here again I suggest that if he refers to clause 9, subclause 3, he will find that a rule for the calculation of the period of separation will perhaps answer his question. If it does not, I will be glad to deal with it again when we are considering that clause.
Referring again to paragraph (c) I would say that the hon. member has given a reason for its usefulness. One can make a distinction, although there is perhaps a certain amount of redundancy. For the clarification and instruction of the parties who will be reading this bill, I think paragraph (c) will be useful because it will cover the case of a person who has disappeared and never been heard of and therefore might be dead. Paragraph (e) would apply to people who are obviously alive. That is part of the answer.
Another part of the answer is that if we struck out paragraph (c) one would not know for sure whether to proceed under paragraph (e) (i) or (ii), because the question would arise whether the disappearance was real and valid, that is, actually a desertion. If the petition was made under (e), the courts would have to make a decision on whether or not there had been a desertion so as to know whether to apply the five year rule or the three year rule. By including paragraph (c), the courts do not have to make this judgment which may be very difficult in the hypothesis of my explanation in respect of the disappeared person who is dead. Such a person would not be known of and the courts could not consult with him or seek information on whether that individual deserted willingly or unwillingly. For these reasons I think the clause is not useless. I agree with the hon. member for Peace River that there is perhaps an element of redundancy regarding paragraph (e), but for the reasons I have given I think it is useful to retain the paragraph.

Mr. Chairman, I am now being asked to interpret statutes other than this one. I do not mind giving advice to such a close colleague. With respect to this bill I would say that the answer is clear. If there has been consummation, no matter what happened later this clause could not apply. I should say that this example is akin to the one given last night where one of the parties is maimed, ill or insane. If the parties continue to live together, as many undoubtedly will, in spite of the fact that one spouse has been disabled, there is obviously no cause for divorce. If they decide, after mature consideration, that they want to obtain a divorce, they will have to go through the same three year waiting period that is necessary when one of the parties becomes incurably insane or incurably ill.
With respect to the final part of the question, whether any other statute would provide for dissolution of marriage in these circumstances, my uninformed recollection is no. Mr. Chairman, in my very limited training I was always taught that a legal draftsman would try to make his bill as clear as possible in the first place so there would be as little room for judicial interpretation and appeal as possible. But now we have the minister telling us that the clause is all right and we will be able to clear up this fuzzy provision because it will be subject to appeal.
I should now like to refer to clause 4(e)(ii). It seems passing strange that there should be a differentiation in respect of the time after

which a person can petition for divorce. The spouse who is deserted can petition for divorce after a period of three years but five years must elapse before the deserting spouse can petition for divorce. This provision implies essentially a trial within a trial. When a person petitions for divorce it must first be ascertained who deserted whom.
What kind of desertion are we referring to in the clause? Are we referring to other acts? In the child welfare act of Ontario "desertion" has one meaning and in most other provinces it has another. What kind of desertion do we refer to in this bill? Do we refer to physical desertion? Suppose a man is married to a shrewish wife and he just walks out of the matrimonial domicile and leaves the wife but continues to maintain her. What is the situation then? She was really responsible for his leaving her. Does this mean the husband cannot petition for divorce for five years but the wife can petition for divorce after three years? Do we mean physical desertion? If one spouse just walks out and leaves the other, does this provision mean he or she incurs an extra penalty?
It would seem to me that clause 4 (e) (ii) is completely redundant. If the clause were passed in its present form all we would do would be to make divorce more expensive to the litigant. I think the clause should provide for three years in either case, in which case, of course, we could withdraw paragraph (ii) completely.

If this honourable house wants to make the period two years, one year or one week, that is a matter for the house and I will not defend the period of three years on the ground of principle. I will not move such an amendment and I do not think I would vote for it, because after comparing the periods which are most acceptable in civilized countries I found that three years was a rather liberal figure.
The fact that this particular form of impo-tency has occurred does not require, it seems to me, that we spell out special treatment in the bill. Surely there is no great difference, at least in principle, between the spouse who cannot have sexual relations for that reason and the one have them because the other spouse happens to be living in an asylum somewhere. I do not think the hardship is greater in one case than the other. The test is whether the spouses are separated. Once again, if three years appears much too long to most hon. members I cannot say that I will defend that period of time on any moral ground, but it seems to me the kind of period we have to impose in order to bring forth the point that a marriage contract is not an ordinary contract and that the state has some interest in it, that society feels that marriages should not be broken off by consent no matter whether one person happens to fall sick or falls prey to an injury, as in the example given. This is my feeling on the matter.
Getting back to the question asked previously, I object to the expression having been used that the subclause is fuzzy. The courts are asked all the time, in respect of all our statutes, to interpret words and questions of fact. It is absolutely inconceivable that any law would be written in such a way that the courts would have absolutely no discretion. I cannot think of a single statute or single code anywhere that does not rely in some instances on an amount of judicial discretion. That is what we have courts for, namely, to apply the law according to their best interpretation. If there was no need for the interpretation of our laws we could have machines to decide these questions. We could put the statute in a machine and the answer would come out. There is always room for a degree of judicial discretion, and because this is the case it does not mean that the bill is fuzzy.

minister has engaged mostly in academic consideration of the law and has certainly not had experience in the practice of advising clients who come to seek advice from counsel or solicitors. Mr. Chairman, I think I will vote against that amendment because it was the intention of those drafting the bill to make a distinction between the offended and offending parties. There was no desire to give any incentive in this bill to the desertion of one spouse by the other. I think the law would be better if we made sure there was no such incentive to desertion. If two parties decide to separate and live apart, for whatever reason, then I suppose that is a fact which the law must accept. This was the reason we wrote this particular concept of breakdown into our law. I think we must be careful not to accept the kind of thinking, generous though it may appear, behind this amendment because once again we are giving an incentive to desertion. I do not believe we should do that. Incidentally, it is for that type of reason we did not accept the recommendation of the joint committee for another kind of breakdown, which was shorter than three years, in a case when there was wilful non-support of either party. We did not want to write into our law any clause which would incline one party not to support the wife, husband or children because such a party might get a quicker divorce and not have to wait for three years. It is for this reason that I, personally, cannot accept the amendment. Once again, I cannot defend my actions on
Divorce Law Reform
any other ground than this which seems to me to be a common sense ground.
While I am on this subject I might answer some of the remarks that have been made about desertion. This is not a new idea we are introducing here for the first time, as some hon. members have said. Desertion is already in our laws because section 2 of the Divorce Jurisdiction Act speaks about desertion. Certainly, the courts have had to interpret this word and they have done so with some differences of opinion among the courts. It is for this reason that the idea of constructive desertion has also been spelled out by the courts.

It is not condonation in the ordinary sense of our statute law. We provide an exception to the ordinary meaning of condonation by saying there can be 90 days of cohabitation without that constituting condonation. We have a long definition here of collusion which is a particular definition that applied to divorce. These are the justifications I give for preferring to stick to these particular words.

The hon. member uses the word "unbearable". When we talk of mental cruelty which becomes intolerable we come in a large degree to the idea the hon. member for Yukon wants to put forward.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North, because it seems to me that it simplifies and clarifies these provisions. I think that is desirable.
The minister, if I understood him aright, said it had been deliberately decided to treat a deserting petitioner differently from one who had just separated without the element of desertion. Perhaps this is reasonable, but I suggest to the minister that the purpose of making these separate categories is clearly carried out in the provisions of clause 9(1) (f) where it is provided that it is the duty of the court:
where a decree is sought under section 4 by reason of circumstances described in paragraph (e) of subsection (1) of that section, to refuse the decree if the granting of the decree would be unduly harsh or unjust to either spouse or would prejudicially affect the making of such reasonable arrangements for the maintenance of either spouse as are necessary in the circumstances.
It seems to me that this provision in the bill would amply take care of the situation where a petitioning husband had deserted his wife and was refusing to make reasonable arrangements for her. I believe it would be a better way of dealing with the matter to leave it to the discretion of the court to say: You, as a deserting husband, are not in a position to secure your divorce; I must refuse it to you under clause 9 because it would be either unduly harsh owing to your conduct or unjust to the spouse you left without provision and would prejudicially affect the making of reasonable arrangements. In addition, under clause 10 and the following ones orders for arrangements can be made.
I suggest that the minister should contemplate the virtues of simplicity in dealing with these matters. He said we should not try to define everything. I am inclined to agree with him on that, but the fewer paragraphs we have about desertion as distinct from separation the better. If we have these provisions about desertion it will just add to the complications where there is a clear case of separation and the court is required to go into the question of whether the husband is

providing adequately for the wife and also whether this was done in the initial instance three years before.
The definition of desertion, however it is made, is a complex and not a simple matter. It is not a question of just physically walking out of the house. I put it to the minister that with respect to all of the offences under clause 3 and the grounds for marriage breakdown under clause 4 there is, with one exception, an opportunity to object. In other words, where the petitioner claims adultery on the part of the other spouse the other spouse has the opportunity to object and to prove that there was no adultery. The same applies to all the other marital offences and the grounds under clause 4 except one, and that is where there is a separation because of the husband or wife being in jail. Then, of course, there is no doubt. There obviously is a separation. A jail term has been handed down and in those circumstances there is no defence of any kind. Thus a divorce will be granted without defence.
I have no particular objection to that but for any of us to think that this bill is going to cure many of the ills present today would be not to face reality. Many of the provisions in the bill have been in force in the United Kingdom since 1937; yet one of the witnesses who appeared before our committee said that 95 per cent of the actions for divorce in the United Kingdom are still based on adultery. The minister will understand the reason for this. Adultery is a very simple thing to prove. There is a claim of adultery, there is an admission of adultery, and that is as far as the court goes. Therefore it is the cheapest and simplest way where a marriage is being put to an end by consent. Where there is no consent, at the present time it is impossible to get a divorce. Under the terms of this bill a divorce can be secured without consent after a period of five years. Other than that I cannot see that the bill changes the picture very much. I cannot see that any judge is going to accept an admission of cruelty, even by both parties. No matter how detailed and long the evidence in the case might be, I submit that what I say holds true. The same might be said about desertion.

I do not wish to labour the point that I originally brought to the minister's attention. His reply indicated that possibly he did not understand my suggestion clearly. I agree with the minister that a three year separation period as a ground for divorce is arbitrary. No one can say whether three years is right or wrong any more than whether five years is right or wrong. That is not the point to which I wish to direct the minister's attention.
My point is that where permanent impotence exists a divorce should be permitted and the parties should not be forced into a period of separation for three years, one year or for any period. I submit that in such cases the marriage should be terminated on the request of the aggrieved spouse without the necessity of any waiting period.
I know that the minister does not lack imagination. Let me refer to circumstances which are likely to exist to illustrate what I am suggesting. Take the case of a marriage which has been consummated and there are children of the marriage and then permanent impotence develops. Under this bill, in order for the wife to obtain a divorce she would have to desert her husband. She might have to take the children with her or leave the children with her husband. She might be without means of support. In any event, she must wait for three years at least before suing for divorce. The bill clearly states that a divorce may be granted after a certain period of separation.

I understand it was this thinking which led the special committee to recommend that a three year period be stipulated, that marriage be considered to have broken down it one of the partners had been deserted for three years or if one had been a deserter for a period of five years. It seems to me that when a marriage is going on the rocks few people will, in fact, be considering these legal distinctions and whether they have to wait for five years or only three years before they can go to court. For those who might be considering their legal rights, it seems to me that the distinction created in paragraph (e) would lead to an undesirable situation in which a husband and wife whose marriage was going on the rocks would be jockeying around to see who was going to desert whom in order that the one deserted could have the advantage of a shorter period of three years before applying to a court. I can envisage that in some situations where hatred runs so high a husband who wanted to leave would refuse to do so and would create hell for his wife in the hope she would desert so that he would be entitled to the advantage of the three year period. For these reasons it seems to me that the distinction created in this paragraph is altogether undesirable, and I hope hon. members will support my amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in connection with subclause 2 of clause 6 there is some doubt in the minds of several members who have read it and reread it concerning what it means. Would subclause 2 of clause 6 result in the recognition in Canada of Mexican divorces or divorces granted by any other jurisdiction outside Canada? At first glance it seems that this subclause is placed here in order to give effect to the first part of the clause relating to the domicile of married women who are under age and married women separate from their husbands' domiciles. However, there does not seem to be any limitation. The wording is most difficult to straighten out. Could the minister either give us the assurance that we will not recognize any divorce granted in any other jurisdiction which does not define domicile as we do, or tell us whether it limits it to places which recognize the domicile of a married woman only?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will gladly answer that, Mr. Chairman. As a matter of fact I stood at the same time as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka because I had an amendment to introduce which I think tends to clarify the very question which has been asked. I realize that since we introduced the bill there have been some questions raised both in the house and in the press about the interpretation of this provision. I should like to distribute copies of this amendment both in French and English. It is seconded by the Postmaster General. I should like to explain here what the intention is and what I believe the amendment spells out. We intend to introduce domicile rules which are new to our law and which will go beyond even the recommendations of the joint committee because we not only apply the new rule of domicile to the married woman within Canada but also outside Canada.
I should begin by saying that clause 6, subclauses 1 and 2, really apply only to married women. In other words, we are not changing the law of domicile as it presently exists for men. That is the reason that in the amendment-hon. members might look at lines two, three and four-I have added these words to the present clause:
-without limiting or restricting any existing rule of law applicable to the recognition of decrees of divorce granted otherwise than under this Act-
Let us sum up the situation in respect of men first. In the case of men the rule will not

change. If a man goes to Mexico, Nevada or anywhere else, that is his domicile if he is domiciled there within the meaning of domicile as given by Canadian courts. Members, especially those who are lawyers, know that this is a difficult term and I would not attempt to define it here because domicile has varying meanings from province to province.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: That is the crux of the issue. It is what the Canadian courts determine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. I do not intend to rewrite all the laws in respect of domicile in Canada. There is a constitutional difficulty involved here. The provinces have their laws in respect of domicile and there has been some difficulty, as hon. members know, with regard to federal statutes in the matter of grappling with this idea of domicile. We did not wish to re-open the debate on that. If a man is domiciled in Nevada he can obtain a divorce under the Nevada laws, but he cannot just go there, establish a short residence there, not domicile in the sense we use the term, come back and expect our courts to recognize his divorce. So for the moment there is no change. Once again may I say that I am not attempting to cover all the jurisprudence and case law in respect of domicile. We are just trying to make the existing rule applicable to women as well as to men.
A woman who is married and domiciled in British Columbia does not have to move to the province where her husband has established his domicile in order to sue for divorce. In other words, under this clause, she is being treated equally with him. I believe this is a step forward toward fair treatment for men and women. We went a step forward and established this rule also in respect of persons domiciled outside of Canada. Here again we are going a bit farther toward liberalism and equality of the parties. We thought that the equality in this regard should apply not only within Canada but also outside Canada. That is the reason for subclause 2. Once again there is no attempt here to solve the problem of domicile in the final sense for men and women. We are just saying that whatever the laws are under provincial statutes or under provincial laws they will in divorce matters be the same for men as for women, a woman being in the position of a man for the purpose of divorce.

speechtext: Before the minister answers I should like to outline one other thing that still puzzles me, and I have in mind the words "without limiting or restricting any existing rule." subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.

Perhaps I may be allowed to answer some of the points, if I am able to do so. In answer to the question as to why we do not settle once and for all the rule of domicile and set it out in this law, apart from the constitutional difficulty, I think it is unrealistic for hon. members to want to settle this kind of extraneous question by the divorce law. I must refer members to the text of the bill which says "for all purposes of determining the marital status in Canada." It is for this purpose alone that I introduced the amendment. This amendment would not apply to other purposes which have to do with income tax, inheritance or anything else. We are saying that the existing laws on domicile, whatever they may be, when you are talking about marriage, will also apply to women.
Surely hon. members are aware of the reason we are doing this. It is not to complicate the law but rather to meet the case of a husband and wife who are living separate and apart. We want to avoid the necessity of a wife having to cross the country or perhaps the world in order to plead her divorce case

December 19, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
in his domicile, which is the case under our present laws. Under our present laws, by and large we define a woman's domicile as that of her husband, if she is married. We are saying that in respect of a divorce which puts an end to the marriage, so far as the establishment of domicile is concerned, a woman can establish domicile in any way which is open to a man. I cannot refer to all the domicile laws in Canada, but if hon. members will look at sections 79, 80 and 81 of the Civil Code of Quebec I think they will find a very satisfactory definition of domicile. We could write this into the statute laws of Canada, but I am not sure that all hon. members would be prepared to do so without having a committee look into the matter. I am suggesting that we bypass this broad definition now and say we are going to accept the laws of domicile but make them equal for men and women.
As to the point of saying "without limiting or restricting" rather then saying "without enlarging", it seems to me the point is we are enlarging the existing rule of law in Canada in such a way that it will apply to women as well as to men. I think that is all we should say at this point.

Mr. Chairman, I can explain the meaning again, but before doing so let me say that when we find the word "domicile" in a Canadian statute-and I gathered from the question of the hon. member for Rosedale that this was understood-the Canadian courts interpret the word according to our law and not according to the law of whatever land is referred to. This explains the meaning of the phrase "domicile of the wife in that country." It is domicile as defined and understood by our courts in connection with our statutes and common law.
This means that if a person goes to Reno and obtains a divorce on the basis of residence and the person is effectively domiciled in Nevada-domiciled, once again, as understood by our courts-we will recognize that divorce because it was granted by a tribunal which had jurisdiction under the law of Nevada. In other words, the Nevada law will apply if the person is resident in Nevada under Nevada law and will be recognized in Canada if the person is domiciled there. Once again, the Canadian courts have always interpreted the word "domicile" in a Canadian statute according to Canadian laws and standards. This is the rule.
I would not mind spelling it out in a clearer way if that is the desire of the committee. I must say that we struggled quite a bit with this wording and I had the assistance of very able draftsmen, especially when there was some doubt after second reading. We then looked at this wording again. If we do not want to meet the kind of problem raised by the hon. member for York East and try to rewrite our laws on domicile, which I suggest we should not attempt if we want to adjourn for Christmas, we must not try to go any further than we do here. We must rely on the Canadian courts to continue interpreting the word "domicile" appearing in Canadian statutes as they have always interpreted it in the past.
With regard to the problem raised by the hon. member for York East, I would refer him to section 80 of the Civil Code of the province of Quebec and let him find the test there, which I think answers his question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my comments on clause 7 will also apply to clause 8. In my opinion neither clause is consistent with the function either of a lawyer or a judge. It is the role of the lawyer to determine the facts in the particular case and to advise his client of their effect under the law. In the role of an advocate it is the duty of the lawyer to adduce proof of facts in support of his client's case and then to persuade the court of his client's rights under the law in the face of these facts.
I should like to turn to some of the considerations which are involved in these two clauses, namely, whether or not a particular couple may be reconciled, whether it would be appropriate to require them to undertake further efforts at reconciliation, and what these efforts should be. In my opinion these are not legal questions and should not properly intrude into legal proceedings. There may be persons with appropriate training in the social sciences capable of prescribing for conduct on the part of either or both the spouses which might lead to reconciliation, and it might well be that following a further study of human relations some more general process of reconciling this type of dispute may be established. I must express some doubt as to the likelihood of finding such an early solution to these problems, but I do not discount the possibility.
I note that the report of the joint committee at page 153 was much less positive than is the draft bill as to the efficacy of this proceeding. The committee acknowledged that compulsory marriage counselling is not a practical proposition and the following statement is made in its report:
However, while the introduction of such provisions into the law might be desirable, it would be a mistake to expect too much from them. The experience in Australia, and some other jurisdictions, would lead one to believe that such powers tend to be exercised infrequently.
It seems clear to me that at the present time members of the legal profession and the bench are not qualified to make definitive judgments on the kind of question which is imposed on them, and it seems likely that the words in the clause which will most frequently be used are the so-called escape words, namely, "except where the circumstances of the case are of such a nature that it would clearly not be appropriate to do so." I have the suspicion that this exception will
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.]
be invoked far more frequently than the other provisions of the clause.
I do not think the clauses impose a serious legal problem or a serious impediment to parliament but I think they are unrealistic. I direct my comment not so much at the minister as at my colleagues at the bar in Toronto who have asked me what we intend to do by this requirement. I do not think these are appropriate provisions. I think I understand some of the minister's thoughts in introducing them but I do not predict legal efficacy for them.

Mr. Chairman, I support the hon. member who has just spoken and I suggest to the minister that the clause be deleted entirely. I urge the committee to vote against this clause. Let us consider it carefully. It reads as follows:
It shall be the duty of every barrister ... except where the circumstances of the case as of such a nature that it would clearly not be appropriate to do so-
Barristers are in business to make money. The old concept of professional ethics has certainly dimmed in the past 10, 15 or 20 years. I would hate to entrust some barristers

with the decision as to which of the circumstances in any case are or are not appropriate. They are not trained to decide that. This is why in subclause 1(a) of clause 7 it is stated:
To draw to the attention of his client those provisions of this act that have as their object the effecting where possible of the reconciliation of the parties to a marriage;
That is easy enough. The lawyer will say to the client: Here is the act, read it. Subclause 1(b) reads:
To inform his client of the marriage counselling or guidance facilities known to him-
I for one cannot even think of one marriage counsellor in Toronto to whom I would care to send anyone. The qualifications of marriage counsellors in Toronto are nonexistent, and complaints have been made about this for years. There are no competent people in this field in Toronto. Of course there are psychiatrists who charge a great deal of money for their services, but I would not suggest to any person that he spend $40 or $50 an hour over a period of several years. Subclause 1(c) reads:
To discuss with his client the possibility of the client's reconciliation with his or her spouse.
I suggest that whatever is usually done by lawyers will be done. I found whenever I undertook to discuss reconciliation with a petitioner for divorce that they had already made up their minds to get a divorce and did not want my advice. Subclause 2 reads as follows:
Every petition for divorce that is presented to a court by a barrister-shall have endorsed thereon a statement by such barrister-that he has complied with the requirements of this section.
I suggest that the compliance will be in word only; it will merely be a rubberstamp compliance. Who will then judge whether the lawyer has indeed complied? Therefore I suggest to hon. members that they should vote against this clause.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Rosedale and the hon. member for Royal put the argument very well. Before the court can look at the petition for divorce the lawyer must advise the petitioners of this concept and the court must be satisfied that it has been considered. We then have a case which amounts to marriage breakdown. I suggest to the hon. member for Greenwood, who is so much in favour of that principle, that he is in favour of these two clauses because they do everything that he feels should be done in so far as the marriage breakdown concept is concerned. Since the house has rejected it and since it would be an unsatisfactory and unworkable way of trying to bring about a divorce, I must agree with the hon. members who support the rejection of these two clauses.

I should like to support the retention of these two clauses. I say to the hon. member who has just spoken that the house has not rejected the principle of marriage breakdown, as I understand it, but has accepted the principle of marriage breakdown as one of the grounds for divorce. The house has rejected the contention of those who wished to have marriage breakdown as the only ground for divorce. The principle of marriage breakdown as an important ground for divorce has been accepted. These two clauses are completely consistent with the principle of marriage breakdown. I hope they will not be treated merely as formality either 
by the legal profession or by the bench but on the contrary will be taken very seriously.
It may well be that at the moment we do not have adequate facilities for marriage counselling, but we have some in the city of Toronto. It is my understanding that they have been effective in some cases. I feel these are important clauses and they should be retained. These two clauses are important and if they prove to be less effective than we think they should be strengthened in the future.

Perhaps I should deal with that point first. As hon. members will recall, when you are in doubt about the meaning of a word in a statute of Canada you look at the translation. The words "barrister, solicitor, lawyer or advocate" are translated into French by the one word "avocat". I think the key to the enigma is that the bar of each province decides who has the right to appear be. ore the court to present petitions for divorce. In some provinces they are called solicitors and barristers. The bar of each province will decide who is entitled to appear and the names given to these people will vary from place to place. I cannot explain exactly why the word "advocate" was used here except that perhaps some provincial bars use the word "advocate". From the context obviously it is any person who is entitled to present a petition for divorce.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
On the same general problem, in dealing with the question of why we talk about reconciliation in these clauses the word "sop" was used. I am sure it was chosen with a little bit of irony. The truth of the matter is
December 19, 1967

that the government took the view that it should write into the bill provisions intended to go as far as possible to avoid divorce by ensuring that reconciliation procedures would be attempted. We did this not as a sop to the very responsible bodies which made representations to that effect but because we wanted to respond as ably as we could to the desire of the Canadian people to maintain marriage as the important institution it is and to put divorce in a very special place in our society. I can say that we went as far as we could under our constitutional authority.
The hon. member for St. Paul's gave the bill his support. I am grateful for his support. He indicated that if it did not go far enough we should try to do better. I agree with his comments. But I can only say here that to go much farther we would have to enter a field which is not strictly a federal field. As I explained in my opening remarks, in this bill we were faced with all kinds of constitutional difficulties, and it would have been simpler if we had sought an amendment to the constitution to transfer jurisdiction over marriage and divorce to the provinces. I hope nobody in the press catches this, but this would have permitted an easier solution of one aspect of the matter because the provinces, through their authority over social welfare, through their authority over the general matter of children, marriage and the consequences of marriage in a social sense, can do much more than we can in the area of reconciliation. Perhaps I should point out, Mr. Chairman, that the first part of my last sentence was partly facetious. We have authority over divorce. We legislate on divorce and we have gone as far as we can to write provisions respecting reconciliation into our laws.
To lessen the fears of the hon. member for Rosedale that we are going outside the spirit of the law by asking the lawyers and the judges to do this, I can only refer him to the laws of a number of countries which are guided by the same rule of law as we have. I would not mention France, which has a different system and which imposes upon a judge the duty to attempt reconciliation, but I would point out that in New Zealand the court is required to consider the possibility of reconciliation, and it may adjourn for that purpose. The adjournment there is for 27 days instead of the 14 days that we have provided. In Australia the court is also required to give consideration to the possibility of reconciliation. Once again, I say we did
Divorce Law Reform
the best we could under our law. Perhaps in better times and under a different constitution we could have a different type of court, similar to those I was attempting to describe yesterday, which would be closer to the concept of administrative law. But once again for constitutional reasons we could not do this.
We felt we must not refuse altogether to tackle the problem, and we have tackled it by a measure that went as far as we felt we could under the constitution. I would gladly accept amendments if they could make it go farther, or I would suggest we take the attitude that, in later years, after some time for study of the application of this legislation, we should see if we can improve it.

It may be that some members of the legal profession will use the escape feature contained in subclause 1. It may be that some lawyers will simply ignore the provisions of clause 7 by consistently using the excuse that in the circumstances of the case it is clearly not appropriate for them to advise their clients that there are marriage counselling services, guidance facilities, etc., available. But in that case, let the onus be on the individual lawyer. Let his conscience bother him. I do not see why we in this parliament should remove the substance of clause 7 simply because it is felt that some lawyers may seek to ignore its provisions.

In connection with this clause I have an amendment to move which I believe to be of some substance. It relates to subclause (1) (a) which provides that when divorce is being considered by a court it shall be the duty of the court to refuse a decree based upon the consent, admissions or default of the parties or either of them, and not to grant a decree except after a trial, which shall be by a judge without a jury.
Here I believe that what was intended was that a decree should not be based upon either written or formal consent presented to the court, or upon mere admissions or default in the absence of a trial. I think it was intended to deal with the question of proof or the manner of proof either of the offence or of the circumstances indicating marriage breakdown. But I would point out to the committee and the minister that a perfectly proper interpretation of the words I have referred to could give them a far wider meaning. They could mean that where there was consent basic to the circumstances concerning the ground for the divorce, the court must refuse the divorce.
It is my suggestion that this weakness could be cured very easily by adding two words to the paragraph which would then read as follows:
It shall be the duty of the court-to refuse a decree based solely upon the consent, admissions or default of the parties or either of them-
And so on. The use of the word "solely" would indicate that it is the intent of parliament merely to deal with the question of how one proves the case upon which a petition for divorce is based, and that the reference is to formal consent or pleadings. This is important because it is quite possible that the intent of parliament could be defeated by some judge who would say that upon the evidence it appears to him that the parties consented, for example, to commit adultery or consented to a separation, and the petition was therefore based upon the consent of the parties.
The fact of the matter is that many divorces under the old system have involved an element of consent. No doubt this will
December 19, 1967

continue to be the case when the new system is introduced. I am not talking about collusion. I am talking about consent to the extent that the parties are in accord as to the facts or are aware of what is going to happen. In these circumstances I suggest it would be useful to clarify clause 9.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether you propose to call it six o'clock and proceed with other business at this stage, but I have an amendment to present to the committee and I will read it in order that the minister may consider it. I move:
That clause 9 (1) (a) be amended and the following substituted therefor:
(a) to refuse a decree based solely upon the written consent, admissions or default of the parties or either of them, and not to grant a decree except after a trial which shall be by a judge, without a jury.

The spokesman for Vawn Pipe Lines made it very clear that while in comparison they may not be as big as Westcoast Transmission they would like to be. This leads me back to the point I was trying to make during an earlier discussion, that by granting to company after company wide open authority and power to build anywhere and everywhere, as

is proposed by the terms of this bill, we are setting up group after group of businessmen who think they are going to be able in effect to run the pipe line business of the country.
By setting up a multiplicity of conflicting and competing interests we will in my view have overconstruction and overexpansion of transportation facilities, in spite of the authority for regulation conferred by the National Energy Board Act. This concern is more pointed if one examines the National Energy Board Act to see what terms of reference are given to the board by that act. As I understand the act, practically no terms of reference are given to the National Energy Board. I other words, it is a board that, subject to the occasional and very spasmodic review of parliament, acts at any particular time in relation to the allocation of certificates for construction of pipe lines almost entirely on the whims or fancies of government policy as they exist at any particular time. This situation is far too closely parallel to the kind of situation which existed in the days of the railways building boom in this country.
The National Transportation Act passed by parliament during the 1966-67 session and as hon. members are well aware, there is reference in that act to pipe lines but pipe lines which are defined strictly as commodity pipe lines. By definition this does not include the kind of pipe lines used for the transmission of oil or gas. It is true there is a preamble to the National Transportation Act which purports to set out a general transportation policy for Canada, but that transportation policy applies only to commodity pipe lines. I do not want to attempt to say whether it is adequate, but as I understand it that is the situation. It applies only to commodity pipe lines which are covered under part II of the National Transportation Act. It does not in any way apply as a term of reference laid down by parliament in respect of gas or oil pipe lines.
This leads me back to the contention that the existing terms of reference in respect of licensing for the construction of pipe lines are not such as to satisfy me that it is advisable or desirable to go on passing bill after bill incorporating companies with wide open authority to construct pipe lines anywhere in the country. In fact, the principle involved in the incorporation of this company is concerned only with the construction of a very modest pipe line within a fairly limited area,

If this is allowed to continue it seems to me it will become virtually impossible for any body such as the National Energy Board or the Canadian Transport Commission to maintain any kind of rationale because of all the conflicting interests and pressures which will be brought to bear.
The concern I am trying to express is by no means frivolous and I am not attempting to express an obstructionist view. I feel that hon. members should give consideration to a broader term of reference than apparently was dealt with by the transport committee. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
With pleasure, Mr. Chairman. I have indicated that this problem deserved consideration and I am happy to be reminded of this by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Forest) at this stage.
I think that if proceedings in separation have been started in the provincial courts with subsidiary or corollary relief concerning the custody of the children, alimony, etc., and that, later, a petition for divorce is introduced and accepted by the courts, it seems to me that when a divorce decree becomes absolute, there does not seem to be any doubt that a divorce having occurred, judicial separation ceases to exist and, as a result, the corollary relief ordered under the separation decree would also cease to exist. In other words, and I base this on the jurisprudence of our courts, when a divorce decree occurs, the bond is broken and there is no longer any question of separation of bed and board because, under the law, there is no longer any marriage.
Therefore, the effects resulting from a judicial separation no longer exist, as would be the situation if one of the parties died. There is a breach of the marriage bond, there is a breaking off of the cause which resulted in subsidiary effects and, therefore, in such a case, the federal act on divorce would prevail, not because of a precedence of the federal act on the provincial act, but because the decree of divorce, once again, destroys the very bond of marriage and thus destroys the effects which may result from a decree of separation. The conflict would be resolved in that way.
The other hypothesis which might be proposed in theory would be: Could the court which granted a decree of separation amend its decree after the divorce? Certainly not, since the divorce ended the marriage.
This brings me to deal with another question raised the other day by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme) about the conservatory measures which can be taken under the Civil Code and the Code of Civil Procedure now in force in the province of Quebec, and which should be taken before the superior court. There is no doubt that those measures of conservatory attachment could not be regulated under our act because, as accurately pointed out by the hon. member, those are measures concerning civil property and rights, and the central
December 19, 1967

government is unable to legislate directly in that field, even if it wanted to. Therefore, the hon. member was right to suggest that, in such a case, the parties in the province of Quebec-and I think that the same reasoning would apply in the other provinces where, as we know, separation legislation exists -should take another petition in separation with the conservatory measures before the civil court, if that were necessary to protect his share of the common property.
This leads us to the conclusion that everything would be much simpler if, first of all, federal legislation regulated not only divorce, but also separation from bed and board. I indicated at the resolution stage that we intended to hold discussions with the provinces in an endeavour to deal with this problem of separation from bed and board and, if possible, treat it in the same way and deal with it in the same legislation as divorce. Secondly, I said that we were hoping the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland would decide to follow the wise advice of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme), according to whom it would be greatly beneficial to the parties if these provinces were to use clause 22 of our bill to allow the superior courts of Quebec and Newfoundland, rather than the exchequer court, to apply the federal legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to reconsider this matter because, without reflecting on the merits or demerits, it seems to me that what is being done by this bill is not only to regularize divorce but make it easier. Earlier in respect of clause 7 and other clauses we had discussion about the obligation which it is suggested falls upon various people to bring about reconciliation, and the criticism that perhaps this is not a proper function to impose upon the advocates who represent the parties in these proceedings, a suggestion with which I concur. If the minister, however, is prepared to impose upon the lawyers the obligation of attempting to bring about a reconciliation- an obligation which may be both too late in time and misplaced after the onus has shifted-then, it seems to me he should also be willing to ensure that the courts will carry out a function, which will now properly belong to the court, not of trying to bring about a reconciliation of the marriage but rather of ensuring that the consequence of the breakup of the marriage does not bring hardship to the children of the marriage.
It seems to me that what is the concern of the clause should be the concern of the bill. I believe that the concern is suggested somewhat casually in a sort of passing fashion in the following words:
Upon granting a decree nisi of divorce, the court may, if it thinks it fit and just to do so having regard to the conduct of the parties and the condition, means and other circumstances of each of them, make one or more of the following orders-

So, it may do so if it thinks fit having regard to the circumstances. There is no obligation upon the court to inquire into the circumstances. There is no obligation upon the court to decide whether the circumstances properly require the making of some order to ensure that the welfare of the children is provided for, and to ensure that there is proper provision for the injured spouse.
What the amendment seeks to do is to ensure that the court, which I submit can discharge this function, will accept as an obligation upon the court the function of ensuring the welfare of the family. The old principle of wards of the court gives testimony to what I am saying. In respect of a bill which is designed to rationalize a divorce, and to ensure that there will be a larger number of cases with regard to which divorce may be granted by the court- divorce having all the consequences it has with respect to the family and children-I suggest it is proper and indeed essential that the legislation should direct the courts to the extent that they will have an obligation to inquire into the circumstances of the family, and make an order accordingly. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in order to bring the matter to a head. I should like to say that I hope the minister will reconsider this matter. I wish to move the amendment which I believe my colleague the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has already read to the committee.

Already I have received correspondence from my constituency which indicates that quite a number of people are pleased with the introduction of this bill. I am sure they will be pleased to hear of its passage. One lady informed me that she thought the minister was a very sensitive, humanitarian intellectual. I thought I would pass that on to him.
As other members have mentioned, it has been more than a quarter of a century since
[Mr. McCleave.J
the last attempt was made to reform the divorce laws of this country. According to the record, Senator Aseltine was able to persuade the members of the other place to pass a measure that would have widened the grounds of divorce to include cruelty and desertion. However, this bill was allowed to expire quietly on the order paper of the House of Commons, without any member even asking a question as to when the minister intended to proceed with legislation.
A very different situation exists today. Since then, public opinion has changed to such an extent that the Minister of Justice has created a precedent in Canadian history by introducing this measure. I am sure that members on all sides of the house will give him credit for that. Politicians from all parties throughout the years have avoided this contentious issue, because it was politically dangerous. We all knew it. In my opinion they underestimated the changing circumstances and opinions in our society, particularly in recent years. It was not until the churches and other organizations and groups in Canada recognized the need for a drastic change in our divorce laws that parliament was persuaded to act in response to public opinion.
In this connection I have had a little research done. This is a matter of historical record which has been passed on to me. Apart from the bill that was introduced by Senator Aseltine in March, 1930, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced a bill intituled "An Act to provide for the Jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada in Matters of Divorce". He introduced that bill continuously from 1949 to 1956. The explanatory note says:
This bill does not change the grounds for divorce. It does not establish divorce courts in Quebec or Newfoundland. It does not make available to persons residing in Quebec or Newfoundland anything not now available to them. It merely transfers the hearing of divorce petitions, in the case of persons residing in these two provinces, from parliament to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
That was a most commendable objective and, in view of the climate of public opinion which then prevailed, that was about as far as anyone would wish to go.
Later the hon. member for Timiskaming introduced a bill a number of times from 1960 to 1966. These provided for changes in the grounds of divorce. The purpose of that bill was to provide a law for the dissolution and annulment of marriage that would be common to all persons domiciled in Canada. That
December 19, 1967

bill widened the grounds for divorce. I must give my hon. friend for Timiskaming credit for introducing his bill continuously from 1960 to 1966.
In 1962 another major effort was made in this house to transfer divorces from the House of Commons to the Senate. The hon. members for Timiskaming and Skeena conducted a filibuster for some months. I know that was very trying for members of the government and for other members on occasion, especially when they had to listen to long extracts being read from the Senate divorce proceedings in order to indicate the need for the change in procedure. I wish to pay tribute to the courage and persistence of those two hon. members. Finally, the government of the day saw the light, gave in and introduced legislation that provided for divorce to be transferred from the House of Commons to the Senate.
As the years went by the courage of hon. members picked up. The public climate was changing also. On February 18 and April 8, 1965, in the new session, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond introduced a bill which would give to the provinces concurrent jurisdiction in Canada and also widen the grounds for divorce. Later, in 1966, the hon. member for Kootenay East introduced his bill. That bill provided for additional grounds for the dissolution of marriage.
As the years went by and as the climate of public opinion changed, as the need for changes in our divorce laws grew, members of parliament responded to that different climate of public opinion by introduction of this legislation.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Later we saw the introduction of a bill by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in 1966-67 to widen the grounds for divorce and make them applicable to all persons domiciled in Canada. Later, the hon. member for York-Scarborough introduced his bill to provide for the dissolution of marriage on a just and common basis throughout Canada. The hon. member told the house in an explanatory note:
Essentially, the grounds for divorce provided for in this bill are adultery, cruelty and desertion, but include involuntary desertion by reason of incurable insanity and three years separation without reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
It is interesting to note that the development of public opinion in Canada has been accompanied by an increasing understanding on the part of members of the house. The
Divorce Law Reform
final act was the introduction of a measure whose committee stage we have now almost concluded.
I wish now to mention one or two other things. On March 15,	1966, the house
approved a motion that a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to inquire into and report upon divorce in Canada, the social and legal problems relating thereto and such other matters as might be referred to it by either house. I was personally very pleased when this committee was appointed, because I have long been of the opinion that committees of the Senate or of the Senate and the House of Commons can undertake investigations into any subject at much less expense than those incurred by some royal commissions. I have read the report of the special joint committee carefully and I must congratulate the joint chairmen, the members of the committee, and the witnesses who appeared before it. I should also pay tribute to the services rendered by the committee's special assistant, Dr. Peter J. King, associate professor of history at Carleton University, and by Mr. Patrick J. Savoie of the Senate committees branch. In my opinion the committee has made a splendid contribution to the understanding of problems relating to divorce in present circumstances.
I heard the minister's speech, I have read it a couple of times and I have listened carefully during the greater part of this debate to what he has had to say by way of explanation of the clauses and in his comments on the various amendments offered. Whether we agree with every detail of what has been done or not, I believe, in all fairness, that we must admire the hon. gentleman for the attitude he has taken toward this legislation and for the spirit in which he has pursued his purpose.
The minister has indicated his willingness to learn from experience in the administration of this legislation and to make improvements or amendments if necessary. In adopting this measure the house will have remedied a quarter of a century of indifference compounded by political apprehension -and we all know what that is in certain circumstances. In conclusion, I say the house has acted with wisdom and prescience to meet a specific human problem which affects a large number of Canadians.

This is something I did not expect, to be frank; I did not think my hon. friend would move so quickly. It is to his credit that he has done so. My hon. friend did say earlier in the debate that he had no vested interest in the subject of this bill. But of course he has, as a member of the Canadian community. And his children, if and when they form families-I am assuming, of course, that he does get married and have children-will be affected by this far reaching measure.
The hon. member for Kootenay West told us he had read the report of the committee. I was a member of that committee and I heard all these briefs presented. We heard presentations from deserted mothers, mothers alone, men, women and judges. But at no time did we hear any evidence as to the effect of divorce on children.
At no time did anyone say a study had been made as a result of which we knew that the effect of divorce on children was so and so. Consequently I rise to say that this bill is not a panacea. It will not result in a greater number of divorces. It will certainly not be a sovereign remedy for marriage or family problems. Indeed, it is but the beginning of new work which we must undertake. We must put our house in order with respect to all matters affecting family units and the rights of children. At the present time the children at least know to what establishment they belong. But we, as a society, having adopted a very liberal view of divorce, have failed to provide a suitable climate for the children of divorced parents; they are still looked upon as being somewhat apart from the rest of the community. They are not yet accorded the same treatment as is accorded to the children of married parents. We have to deal with this situation because these are the children affected by the legislation we are passing.
I hope the minister's next endeavour will be to continue research into the problems of divorce as they affect the children, and into the whole field of the laws relating to divorce proceedings.
