subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a number of us who did not have the opportunity to speak on second reading. There are some of us, I believe on both sides ef the house, who have some ideas we would like to put forward. We understand, because of the resignation of the former president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that a new president is to be appointed very shortly. Numerous rumours have been circulated to the effect that a very highly respected and very senior civil servant will be appointed to this position.
All members of the house are cognizant of the fact that the new president of the C.B.C. may be faced with problems which he or she has never experienced previously. I think it is only proper that the person who takes on this very important job should have the opportunity of receiving suggestions from members of this house. I know, Mr. Chairman, that suggestions from members of this house are not welcomed by the senior officials of the C.B.C. and that when one does offer suggestions which are not welcome they are not taken very kindly.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We hope when this broadcasting act passes many of the complaints about the C.B.C. will disappear. Let that not be a fond hope. Perhaps the new president will be able to spruce up his policies. I am sure this will be acceptable to the Secretary of State and, indeed, to many members of this house, and the country. Perhaps many of the faults which have caused the complaints over the years can be rectified.
5640	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
There has been created an impression in the public mind, through the press, periodicals and the like, that a number of members of this house are opposed to the C.B.C. as such. There may be some who are, but I for one have been accused repeatedly of this and I am not opposed. I think the corporation performs an excellent and valuable service to the country and can continue to do so. What I object to are some of the policies that have been carried out in some branches of the C.B.C. It is those policies which over the years have caused the vast majority of complaints. I am sure it is the hope of many members of this house, as it is mine, that these complaints which I intend to deal with specifically, can be rectified in future so that the C.B.C. can continue to serve Canada.
There have been many complaints raised about the intellectual entertainment programs. I do not suppose it is easy to please completely any two people in the country, because one is pleased by something while another is pleased by something else. This is because people have different tastes and like different things. I do not intend to make any comment about the general level of the quasi-intellectual entertainment programs of the C.B.C. Some people like them and some do not. Personally I like the majority of them but I may be unique in this respect. The only suggestion I would make is that it is obvious some of the producers of the entertainment programs for the C.B.C. lack the same standard of taste which is generally acceptable in Canada. I hope the new president puts his foot down and will insist that some of these producers will accept these general standards. Perhaps they feel these programs are acceptable because of a new spirit of permissiveness in Canada, but since it is the public which must pay for them, they should have some regard to general standards of behaviour. I hope this will be borne in mind by the new president, and some of these producers who I think produce these programs for no other purpose than to show off and to shock the public.
Another complaint on the part of many members of this house, including myself and many members of the general public who have brought this to my attention, concerns the public affairs programming of the C.B.C. It is in this regard I have serious complaints which fall generally under three headings. The first relates to political interference on the part of the C.B.C., and a heavy political bias in respect of many public affairs programs.

DEBATES	December 19, 1967
The second group of complaints relate to matters of public controversy such as the Viet Nam question, race riots and apartheid, to mention a few. Unfortunately the C.B.C. seems inevitably to present only one side of a question. Any opposing point of view is presented in such a biased manner it cannot be considered a fair presentation.
The third group of complaints relate to the deliberate and fraudulent misrepresentation of the credentials of speakers. This can also be said of photographs and other things. I hope all these complaints can be avoided. If the causes can be corrected I am sure the complaints will disappear. It goes without saying that any member of this house would strenuously object to any outside political interference in the C.B.C. At the same time I think it is proper to object to political interference, or that which appears certainly to be political interference, from within the C.B.C. itself.
I have no hesitation in saying that on rare occasions it may seem that a point of view of the Liberal party or the Conservative party is presented by the C.B.C., but most people to whom I have talked regard the C.B.C. as a propaganda machine for the N.D.P. All one has to think of is the interviews by Mr. Laurier LaPierre and Mr. Pierre Berton. I have several examples of this.
During the 14 or 15 years I have been a member here I have driven back and forth between my constituency and Ottawa on innumerable occasions. During those trips I have listened to the C.B.C. constantly and made notes on every occasion. I have a file containing hundreds of examples. If any member of the C.B.C. would like to discuss these with me privately on some occasion I would be only too happy to accommodate him.
The general impression created is that the point of view of the N.D.P. is greatly overemphasized out of all proportion to the number of its members in this house and its percentage vote in the country. That party is promoted steadily in every conceivable field of public affairs. Let me make it quite clear that I have no objection to N.D.P. propaganda on C.B.C. My objection is that the two major political parties receive almost no time in this regard. After all, the supporters of the Liberal and Conservative parties pay the taxes that keep the C.B.C. going, and this situation does not seem fair.
My next point relates to this same matter, I refer to the one-sided point of view on
December 19, 1967

matters of public controversy. The parliamentary secretary to the present Prime Minister in a speech in Winnipeg pointed this fact out very well. That speech has been quoted at length by other members of this house including the hon. member for Athabasca, the hon. member for Leeds and I believe the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I can only say that when you receive one-sided views on race problems in the United States, or the Viet Nam situation, it does not help the public reach a reasonable conclusion.
Most of us in this house have had the opportunity from time to time of talking with fairly senior people in the C.B.C. I have had the viewpoint expressed to me on many occasions that it is not the function of the C.B.C. to present a balanced picture of such controversies, but to lead the people in thinking in the proper way. It would seem to me that on matters of great public interest and controversy such as the Viet Nam situation, a balanced point of view should be presented so the public could draw its own conclusions as to who is right and who is wrong. This is difficult to do at the best of times, but when you get only one side of the picture the brain washing effect is pretty evident.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
This leads me to a question in respect to the commentators on C.B.C., and this matter relates also to the previous point. I refer to the falsification of the credentials of those people who speak on C.B.C. I have here a good many examples of this, some of which I have heard and seen myself, and others that have been brought to my attention. I will give just two illustrations which might be of interest to the house. The first is this. A few years ago on the program "Preview Commentary", which I think is described as a free expression of opinion, whatever that means, on a good many occasions we heard one, Professor Michael Oliver, giving a commentary on the news. He was described as a professor of political science at McGill University. Some thought it strange that no professor of political science of any other university was ever called upon to comment.
We later discovered that this gentleman was elected president of the New Democratic party. He continued for some time on the C.B.C. to give commentaries on the news, as Professor Michael Oliver. As a matter of fact these commentaries were very interesting, but I just wonder what would have been said

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting from some quarters of this house if the president of the Liberal association or the president of the Progressive Conservative association had been brought on to "Preview Commentary" to comment freely on the news every morning. I can imagine the comments that would have come from some of my friends to the left, had this taken place. This is just one illustration.
I will give another example which I think is a really interesting one. This occurred several years ago when I happened to be at the United Nations. It was brought to my attention that a television show which had been produced in Toronto was exceedingly critical of the entire Canadian delegation at the United Nations, its activities and the personnel thereof. At that time the Toronto Globe and Mail published an editorial and said that ordinarily, from their information, they would not have thought this to be so, but since the speaker on the television show, Mr. Arnold Beichman, was described on the C.B.C. as the United Nations correspondent of the Christian Science Monitor, they must pay attention to it.
I was quite familiar with members of the press gallery of the United Nations and made inquiries about this matter. I asked whether Arnold Beichman, who was described by the C.B.C. as United Nations correspondent for the Christian Science Monitor, in fact held that position. I was told he had never worked for the Christian Science Monitor, was not a member of the United Nations press gallery, never had been and was not known to the press gallery. The C.B.C. were contacted and said they had made a little mistake and it would not occur again. About three weeks later, on a television program advertised in the Globe and Mail, the program being about anti-Americanism in Canada, I noticed that on the panel were Mr. A, Mr. B, Mr. C, and Mr. Arnold Beichman the United Nations correspondent for the Christian Science Monitor. So there was no possibility at all of a second mistake having been made by the C.B.C. As it turned out Mr. Beichman was apparently editor of the "AFL-CIO" News Bulletin.
These are just illustrations, Mr. Chairman, and I have many more here, of what can only be described as misrepresentation of the credentials of people who appear on the C.B.C. I have another illustration. Not too long ago there was on the C.B.C. a program about the Viet Nam war. Certainly the suffering of individuals on both sides is a subject
December 19, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting of pity and concern to everybody. There were televised a number of pictures purporting to show atrocities in Viet Nam which undoubtedly resulted from bombing. One picture shown on this program was of a small child covered with black as a result of an explosion, sitting on the steps of a building crying and obviously covered with blood. It was a very moving picture indeed.
There was only one thing wrong. Those of my vintage and others perhaps remember that this was one of the leading propaganda pictures of world war II. It was a picture which appeared on the cover of Life magazine at the time of the bombing of Chungking. It may be said that this was just the kind of thing that happened in Viet Nam, but it was represented as having taken place in Hanoi.
This is what we have complained about so often in the house. Attention is never paid to complaints made in the house. Impertinent telegrams are sent by officials of the C.B.C. and summonses are received to appear in their office to discuss the matter with them. There is a gap between members of the house and the C.B.C. It may be that C.B.C. officials feel they are unfairly treated, that there is a lack of dialogue, although I hesitate to use the word, and "conversation" may be a better word in this context. Perhaps officials of the C.B.C. feel there is lack of conversation between members of the house and the C.B.C., but I feel that the public which has to foot the C.B.C. bills to a tune of $140 million or $150 million a year should at least be permitted to express its views through members of parliament to the Secretary of State, who is in charge of the C.B.C. and who can then relay these viewpoints and complaints to the corporation.
Naturally no one expects the management of the C.B.C. to pay attention to every single complaint which comes in. Every one knows that is impossible. But one does expect a slightly more courteous hearing of these complaints. I can only hope that when the new president of the C.B.C. and the new senior officials take over, these serious complaints, whether they are made by members of the house as individuals or on behalf of their constituents, will be given serious consideration. No one wants to hamstring the management of the C.B.C. I imagine it is probably difficult to administer such a large corporation. However, I think the management should pay some attention when complaints are made with regard to the political bias of certain broadcasts of the news and one-sided


presentations are made of matters of great public concern. The C.B.C. management should then make some effort to bring some of the producers to heel.
I should like to make one more comment. It has always puzzled many of us why some subjects which have no direct bearing on Canada are dealt with at such length by the C.B.C., a good example being the racial disturbances in the United States. Naturally these matters are of some interest to Canadians, because the United States is our next door neighbour and we have been tied up with them one way or another. It is natural that what goes on there is a matter of great interest in Canada. But when day after day and hour after hour we get nothing but pictures of racial disturbances in Alabama or in Cleveland, it becomes rather much. Someone has suggested to me that perhaps one of the reasons for the emphasis on this subject is that since a great many of C.B.C. radio broadcasts permeate a large section of the United States, and so do some of our television programs, perhaps some of these programs are really being directed at the United States and not at Canada. Be that as it may, and even if the intention is to direct some of these programs at the United States in an effort to reform them or change their attitude, the fact to be remembered is that we are paying for the programs. If anyone is going to reform the United States, they had better do it themselves. I am not suggesting that such programs should not be broadcast. I think that anything that goes on in the United States is of interest here, but it does not warrant so much C.B.C. time. I think this matter should be reviewed.
I know other hon. members will wish to comment on this subject and I intend to bring my remarks to a conclusion. Let me just make it clear that I am very much in favour of the C.B.C. and I like the great majority of its programs. I think they are excellent and the C.B.C. should be commended for them. I refer particularly to some of their artistic and sports programs. However, with regard to public affairs programs I hope the new president and the senior management of the C.B.C. will pay a little attention to some of the complaints that have been made in the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not going to make a general speech at this stage; I was prepared to speak on particular clauses of the bill. However, having heard the number
December 19, 1967

of shots fired by the hon. member for Oxford I have come to the conclusion that some of them require a reply.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
If the hon. member is a friend of the C.B.C., all I can say is God protect the C.B.C. from its enemies. I got the impression that he would like a broadcasting corporation which did nothing controversial and which had lots of commentators expressing views which he liked. Then there would be no problems. It is some news to us that the C.B.C. is the political arm of the New Democratic party. I have a great deal of evidence to the contrary. I wish I could show the hon. member the thick file of correspondence which has passed between the leader of our party in the province of Saskatchewan and the president of the C.B.C. He would know that gentleman, in any event, does not consider it to be the political arm of the New Democratic party. A number of my colleagues in the House of Commons, when they get fed up, say the C.B.C. is just a bunch of Liberals. Perhaps this is the way it should be: Keep everybody guessing. I can assure you if the C.B.C. is the political arm of the New Democratic party they are not serving us the way we would like them to.
The hon. member for Oxford is also asking for a balanced view on race relations in the United States and conditions in Rhodesia. He will have a hard time finding many public spokesmen in Canada who will express opinions he may like to hear on these subjects. I should like to say a word or two, Mr. Chairman, about the proposed new appointments of president and executive vice president of the C.B.C. I imagine that the announcement of these appointments will be made after the house has recessed. The Prime Minister did say that he would make the announcements after the bill had third reading. There is not very much time and, as I say, I suppose these announcements will not be made until perhaps next week or the week after. We have heard reports concerning the names of two gentlemen who have been suggested for these positions. They are both highly qualified in the field of administration and have proven themselves respectively in the public service and in private business. Without saying anything detrimental about either of the two gentlemen suggested, I should like to say it is a pity neither of them has any experience in broadcasting. I think one of the two should have had broadcasting experience.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Broadcasting is a complex field and the C.B.C. is a complex organization. It would have been better if one person had had experience in broadcasting. Again, these appointments have not been made as yet and we are only going on rumour. I hope that the new heads of the corporation, whoever they may be, do not try to put their feet down too heavily, as the hon. member for Oxford suggested they should. If the C.B.C. ever reaches a stage where they do not do things that annoy members of parliament or annoy the public, where they do not do challenging, controversial things, then I do not know what we will need them for. I hope we will have a public broadcasting corporation that will continue to put on public affairs programs, entertainment programs, that will challenge the people, that will please some people and that will annoy others.
I recall, Mr. Chairman, about 20 years ago when I was living in Ottawa Max Ferguson began broadcasting. At that time he imitated some members of parliament, and I believe they got up in the house and complained about the kind of thing this man was doing on C.B.C. radio. We need people who will poke fun at us, who will challenge us, who will present conflicting points of view. The experience has been that this is much more likely to happen on a public broadcasting system than on private broadcasting. I hope therefore, that the new heads of the corporation will perhaps make organizational changes which may be necessary, effect economies which may be necessary, but leave a free rein to the producers who produce the kind of programs which will interest and arouse the people of this country. Otherwise, it would be a very tame body and would not be serving the purpose at all.
I should like only one other comment on the remarks on the hon. member for Oxford. He based his whole statement upon the fact we are paying for this public broadcasting service and therefore we have a right to speak. This is true. We are paying also for private broadcasting. If the hon. member would look at the information supplied by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for 1965 he would see that a total of $162 million was spent on radio and television advertising in Canada.

We are talking about the Broadcasting Act which deals with all of

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks about this broadcasting bill which is now before us again after having been referred to a committee and reprinted following several essential amendments. At first sight, some of those amendments seem rather minor ones, even though a few are somewhat interesting.
I should like to refer particularly this evening to clause 2. My remarks may seem of a general character, but they will deal mainly with that clause of the bill.
For many years, Canadians have been asking for radio and television services everywhere and in all areas. That is to say that this medium of information, of culture and of recreation is quite highly esteemed by the public. For those reasons, then, I feel this bill must be studied and passed as soon as possible, because it seems to make the necessary changes.
Once this new act is passed, the committee entrusted with managing the broadcasting system, private as well as public, can then satisfy the request of Canadians who have been clamouring for radio and television services. In this connection, I should like to point out that too many fairly important centres are still deprived of the services of this system or this means of information.
[Mr. Prittle.l
I recall that, in 1962, when I was elected for the first time, I noticed that certain areas in my riding had made application and had brought pressure to bear, to get the services of the C.B.C. Not long after the 1962 selection, we were faced with a severe austerity program and, at that time, the millions of dollars granted the C.B.C. for its expansion were withdrawn, and the C.B.C. could not provide the additional services it had intended to give. Therefore, as a result of that austerity program, of that financial crisis, areas such as Chibougamau, Chapais, Clova and many others, throughout the country, were refused radio and television coverage because of a lack of money. Therefore, year after year since then, those developments have always been postponed due to a lack of money.
Once again this year, following the announcement made a few days ago by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), the same situation prevails and the citizens who live in those regions, which the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) like to call remote regions, isolated regions which cannot be reached or can be reached only with great difficulty, will have to wait again, in short will have to wait again until the government finds the necessary funds to give them that service.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, when the ministers or the government tell us that those regions are remote, isolated and, thus, inaccessible, I disagree with such statements because when it comes to collecting taxes there, the Minister of National Revenue does not find them too remote. The miners who live in those regions know that very well, for they have to pay twice over for services which they do not get because, as pointed out by the hon. member who spoke before me, television, whether public or private, must be paid for.
Therefore, when the people of those regions buy a bar of soap, a pack of cigarettes or any other product advertised on television, they pay a slightly higher price because the companies which advertise their products on television raise their prices to pay for the publicity. Therefore, these people are paying for television services which they do not get. This is an injustice which I hope will be corrected by the new broadcasting council. I think that the hon. Minister of Finance should be approached as soon as possible by the Secretary of State, so that the
December 19, 1967

C.B.C. may obtain the appropriations it needs to extend its services in all parts of the country, so that as many Canadians as possible may enjoy them, as well as private stations. We note that private enterprise can hardly serve those places, and it is up to the C.B.C., which is a crown corporation, to give those services.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is another point which I would like to raise this evening. I referred to it a few days ago and I would like to bring it up again this evening. In some areas such as the one in which I live, the northwestern area of the province of Quebec, we have a private radio and television station. However, as that service does not entirely meet the requirements of the public and broadcasts programs which sometimes people can hardly understand, because they are unsuitable, I ask the C.B.C. to extend the services of FM radio, in order that we may obtain some truly cultural programs which could be heard by everyone, by those who prefer good music, first-rate music rath-em than music which I would compare to abstract art music which means just about nothing and only produces headaches and some rhythm.
So, I think that the C.B.C. should provide the northwestern region of Quebec, the region of Abitibi, with FM radio service so as to serve the public as well as possible.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, on clause 2 of the bill, I am wondering about subclause (i) stating that:
-service should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for educational broadcasting;
I should like to ask the Secretary of State if there is an agreement with the province of Quebec, because I believe that, in matters of education, the government of the province of Quebec is rather touchy, and rightly so. I think that agreements should be reached by the two governments so as to avoid any encroachment.
Mr. Chairman, in closing my remarks, I hope that the minister will pay them particular attention and that the C.B.C. particularly will have available the necessary money to extend broadcasting services everywhere in Canada.

I submit it will do justice to neither.
To return to my point, I am much concerned about this undiscussable area in the C.B.C. It was not discussed in the committee to any extent. At the beginning of the sittings, every time we came to one of these difficult, dangerous or possibly embarrassing aspects, the clause was allowed to stand. We were told this had been done so that the committee could get on with the housekeeping part of the subject and that at the end there would be time for a complete discussion of these problem areas. Of course when we did eventually reach that point, passage of the bill through committee was drastically accelerated as a result of the resignation of the president of the C.B.C. and the urgency of rushing ahead with the legislation so that the nation could cease holding its breath and learn who the new president was to be.

All the clauses which had been allowed to stand were rushed through in a single afternoon, with the bare minimum of discussion. I felt this was a regrettable and reprehensible use of the committee. We hear a lot about what the committee system can do for parliament generally, but if we continue doing to the committee system what we are doing to it now there is not much hope in that direction.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I should like to talk about what I would call the sweet smell of decay which has surrounded a good part of the supposedly entertainment programming of the C.B.C., particularly in some of its most prestigious spots on the prime time. I know the minister has received letters about some of these programs and I know other members as well as myself have received such letters also. Previously I was one of those people who defended the program "Festival" particularly. I took the position that the good things it did were quite capable of balancing out the odd utter failure that would happen every so often. But I do not think that ever before in the history of our Canadian broadcasting have we seen such a lengthy process of assault on the sensibilities of the Canadian public as we have through this fall and early winter season of the C.B.C.
In spite of the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond I do not quite see why the public should have to sit back and in a sense allow itself to be hammered over the head by material that is pointless, tasteless, provocative and expensive or have to turn it off after they become sick of writhing as they watch it, knowing that they are paying for it through taxation. Although the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond may equate the sums which go through by the means of advertising into program production to those which come through the public purse, I do know that although you can stop buying the product-you do not have to buy the soap or detergent or whatever it may be-you cannot stop paying taxes. At least I have not found a method of doing so yet and I doubt whether the minister has either.

I would entirely agree with the minister in that regard.
I should like to quote from an article written by Mr. John Sparrow which appeared in the Sunday Times of London, England. In a sense speaking to today's public and using

examples drawn from samples of Swift and Burke he says:
"You have subtilized yourselves," he might tell with Burke, "into savages," pointing to two revolutions that are taking place within our gates: the Abdication of the Artist and the Abdication of the Adult.
The abdication of the artist means the triumph of Anti-Art; the domination, in literature and in music, in painting and in sculpture, of a random element. The chance object usurps the place of the artefact; finding is making; the spectator takes over from the artist, the audience from the composer and the executant. If the artist asserts himself at all, it is not to carry out a conscious purpose, but to fulfil an inner impulse which he does not seek to control.
In all this Swift might see a revolt against the rule of order of design, of restraint; a deliberate appeal to chaos and an invitation to violence; a challenge to the very idea of art as a special kind of conscious activity.
He then went on to say that through this abdication by the artist we have a policy of simply presenting life as it is without expurgation and with a minimum of editing. The article then continues in this regard:
-an aim which, if its validity is admitted, justifies not only the presentation of the random "happening" as a work of art, but the description in print, and the representation, (even, perhaps, the actual exhibition) on the stage, of copulation, excretion, sadistic practices, anything, in short, that people do.
Later the article states:
All this Swift might well observe and record with an amused and perverted relish. His scorn he would reserve for the abdicators-
Mr. Sparrow lists them as critics, instructors, parents and legislators. He then says:
-who might well appear to him to have lost, in a paralysis of confidence, the will and the power to criticize, to control, to condemn; and that, at the very juncture when civilization and enlightenment are under the heaviest attack.
I am afraid that through the rising processes and through the timing the government has used in presenting this bill for study this chamber will find its members among the legislators who are abdicators. This area will not receive the consideration and the discussion it should, and because of a paralysis of hesitation we will withdraw from the attempt to regulate and to call, through the legislation itself, for a little more order out of the chaos.
You might feel that these words are a little harsh. Let me quote from the C.B.C. Times itself, which is not usually regarded as the most severe critic of the C.B.C. Let me quote from the previews they gave of three of the programs which followed in a series and had
December 19, 1967
a rather cumulative effect on the public. I begin with a review of something called "The Ernie Game". It states:
"The Ernie Game is very modem, very contemporary-the things that it deals with are things that are the preoccupation of the psychedelic generation ... sanity, insanity, consciousness."
These are quotations from what was said by Mr. Owen, the producer. It continues as follows:
I'm presently very much interested in surfaces. I think that's where the profundity is-in the surface, that there is only a surface, that the other thing is an invention ... In The Ernie Game, which is all surface, nobody ever tells you anything about the characters, no information is provided, the reason for doing anything is completely unclear, because I think it never is clear.
I have no objection at all to the artist having a private insight or playing a private joke on the public, but I do question the advisability, the desirability and the propriety of asking the taxpayer to foot the bill constantly and regularly without being able to obtain anything from it.
Let us look at the description of "Waiting for Caroline" from the C.B.C. Times a week or two later. It states in part:
It's not, however, just a simple love story. That's something Kelly says he's not interested in filming.
The last thing I want to do is entertainment," he says. "Unless one stimulates an audience to be aroused rather than to be more soporific, it's a waste of time.
I think people should come away with their complacencies somewhat jarred."
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
I must admit that it stimulated the audience. It stimulated people to write letters to me and, I am sure, to a great many other members of parliament. These people are aroused because they are being asked to pay for this form of stimulation.
I should now like to refer to the final effort of this series, called "The Paper People". One director described it in the C.B.C. Times in these words:
-light, gay, frivolous, but underneath is an edge of despair and terror. I have been told it has the baroqueness of a Fellini production, and the mysticism of some of Antonioni's work. It's not an historical piece. It's very contemporary and avant garde, about the "now" generation.
The description continues in this way:
It's a slice through the artsy crowd. To some people it may seem sick, a little camp, a bit decadent. But it's really a rather strange love story, and a search by the artist for many things.
I submit that when the C.B.C. in the C.B.C. Times calls its own programming
on Broadcasting decadent and suggests that it may seem sick and a little camp, it really is, and that we have it on the best authority. We have noticed this fall something that has been missing from the Canadian television scene, that is, a revolt amongst the critics themselves who have grown weary of calling this sort of programming harmless, artistic, very fine. They have grown weary of seeing the same bedroom scene over and over again, week after week, regardless of what is the title of the production. The undressing of the characters in the bedroom scene has not been sufficient to add that much interest to the program, and it has reached the stage where the critics now describe this scene as the "obligatory" scene; it has to be in or it will not be a C.B.C. production.
I should like to quote one critic who reviewed "The Paper People", the last of this series of programs, and described it as "pretentious, sickeningly arty, and boring." Sheila H. Kieran says:
I've always considered myself one of that band .. who have thought of the C.B.C. as a noble experiment and who have looked down on its detractors as Philistines ... but, boy, is the C.B.C. making it hard.
This was because she had seen the screening of "The Paper People". She went on to say:
Yesterday I saw a screening of "The Paper People", next Wednesday's Festival production. Even for the precious types who inhabit the C.B.C. this play is a bit much: it is pretentious, arty-in the worst sense-and downright boring.
Most of all it is insufferably arrogant-it seems to have been made by the few for the few. I don t subscribe to the idea that everything the C.B.C. does has to have the widest mass audience but, with this production, the C.B.C. becomes the world's only national network serving 50 people.
I think that is a rather good line, because I understand this final production of the series cost $150,000. This figure has been mentioned in various reviews on the program. At a time when we have heard an appeal for austerity, which has great merit, and the government has seen fit to take the subsidy off quality farm products, I wonder whether it might not consider that it is too highly subsidizing in the C.B.C. a product singularly lacking in quality. Sheila Kieran talks about "the characters standing around and talking significantly." Then she says:
-frankly, I still don't know what they were talking about. (I have a sneaking suspicion they don't know either.)
I might tell the minister that I was invited out for dinner the evening this production

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting was to appear, and so I hesitantly asked my host and hostess if we could not watch "The Paper People" because I was concerned about it. I knew it was the third part of a trilogy and I thought I should at least see it before I rose to criticize it in the House of Commons. Very graciously they consented to watch it. I am still apologizing in a way for the imposition on those who were entertaining me that evening, because if Sheila Kieran whose business it is to write about it did not know what they were talking about, then certainly the average Canadian or even the considerably intellectual Canadian failed to know what they were talking about.
I know the minister has received strongly worded letters about the program. I will quote from one, a copy of which I have received. The program commenced with a warning that this is adult entertainment, and perhaps one should shut it off. As the writer points out, this was a slightly pompous warning. She went on to say:
Did anyone think of the myriads of 13-18 years group baby sitting, watching their own T,V.'s or otherwise out from under adult supervision? What are you trying to do to them? They are struggling into a strange complex adult world and these are the guide lines they are offered.
Here the author was referring to the program "Waiting for Caroline" but I am sure the confusion was compounded a week or two later by "The Paper People". She went on to say:
In our youth certain people undoubtedly behaved like this but their example wasn't thrown at us and depicted as the adult, glamorous, ''in" way to conduct our lives, by a communications medium that subtly affects us all. All youth is not yet decadent and corrupt. Their decency amazes one. But what chance are we giving them, depicting licentiousness as freedom, self discipline as a quality completely unknown and truth in personal relationships not even to be considered.
I repeat, where is the C.B.C. leading these people who will take Canada into the second century? Don't underestimate your influence.
I would suggest that in the final stage of considering the legislation we should give serious thought to amendments which will set down a little more firmly guide lines for the Canadian radio television council not only for C.B.C. broadcasting but also in the private area, because I think it is important for us not to abdicate this great responsibility. I feel the council is far too small in number to adequately take care of all the housekeeping duties which the bill assigns to it. The members of the council will scarcely be sufficiently representative to include representation of the areas most concerned

DEBATES	December 19, 1967
about the moral and religious well-being in the country, and I suspect they will spend their time setting down regulations about how many minutes of advertising should be allowed per hour, about which station should be licensed where, and about how much colour we should have in television programs,-in other words about housekeeping and not about programming.
Unless we provide in the bill more guide lines than are contained in it at present, I am afraid the council will have few occasions to consider seriously the impact and the purpose of the productions that are, after all, what broadcasting is all about.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
It bothers me when I receive a letter such as the one from which I have quoted, and I am sure my experience is repeated throughout the house. I experience a tremendous sense of helplessness in the face of such a letter. It is not a letter from a crank. It is a letter from an intelligent, articulate, reasoning and concerned person who wants to know what can be done. I have received many letters like it in the last two years.
I think there is something that can be done without in any way impinging on the artistic freedom of the producers and artists. If they are truly artistic they will learn to select and they will discipline themselves. They will find that, by selection, the meaning is increased and not decreased. Without impinging unon their artistic prerogatives at all, we can set down guide lines that will express the wishes of the voiceless mass of Canadians who sense something is wrong and who have felt up until now they just could not get at that something which is wrong. We can express concern for the sensitivities of religious groups, of parents and of those who are concerned with the moral development of the young. We can do this as legislators in this parliament.

As has been pointed out on numerous occasions, there is no T.V. station owned by the C.B.C. in that area. The result has been that we find it difficult to receive adequate C.B.C. coverage in many areas of the province. The intention was to put a station in Saskatoon but because of the freeze on certain areas of the dominion, including Saskatoon, nothing was done for about two years. Finally the matter was brought before the Board of Broadcast Governors back in March and approval was given in April for the construction of the station in Saskatoon.
This matter then went to the cabinet. I am astonished that it has taken the cabinet some months to make a final decision upon whether or not they would proceed with the building of this station, since it had been obvious for at least four years a station was needed in that area. Yet in spite of that, nothing was done. Now we are caught in the so-called economy squeeze, and nothing is going to be done in the immediate future. The people in this portion of the west to which I refer might accept this decision more readily if they did not feel there had been a great deal of money wasted by the C.B.C. in launching coloured television. I will not say that money is actually wasted, but when some $30 million odd goes into colour television and we do not have adequate black and white television it can be understood that we in that area are a little bit incensed. Furthermore, when we realize that the C.B.C. spent some millions of dollars giving television coverage to Expo we are somewhat disturbed that our area of the country is being forgotten.
